items.title: Show HN: Get your coding agent off ~2019 JavaScript, onto modern web primitives
items.summary: Browsers natively handle a lot of what used to take 50 lines of JS (or a dependency): `CSS.highlights` for text range highlighting without s everywhere, ` ` and showModal() give you backdrops and ideal focus management, `field-sizing` to auto-grow textareas as the user types.. (Something yesterday's ftrain post touched on [0]) Models know about some of these by name, but consistently won't default to using the platform-native solution and instead prefer the incumbent +JS based pattern. We started an effort in Chrome to supplement coding agents with this key domain knowledge and we're shipping our 1.0 today, in collaboration with Firefox, MDN, and Edge. 200+ guides (~1.7MB) of curated, hand-crafted implementation best-practices from web experts, updated as the web evolves. (Open source, obv, so.. we'll welcome your bikeshedding ;) Readable versions here: [1] I've spent the last 9 months obsessing over how to ship this as an agent skill + (Agentic RAG) CLI without blowing up your context window. (Or cedeing activation mechanics to MCP dynamic tool search). The skill description is minmaxed for activating on relevant frontend tasks. The RAG work I'm pretty proud of… originally a 500mb native stack down to a ~7MB pure-JS package, ~10ms search on your CPU. We just introduced a deterministic 'legacy-scan' (trained on 30k github repos) to identify old 'n dusted patterns that your agent can modernize. (92% avg precision on held-out repos.) People make a lot of claims about what coding agents are good/bad at. We wanted receipts, so we invested heavily in eval infra [2] to help us hill-climb, but also to identify when knowledge is common enough we can prune our guides. (Ofc, some of the things we thought AI didn't know turned out to be wrong :) We run codex/claude/agy against 200 tasks without the skill and then with.. In total ~1,700 playwright/AST-based assertions. Agents go from 55% pass unguided to 92% guided. Try it out: DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest install DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate dialog modal" DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan ./src If you spot something wrong or weird, give us a holler! Longer write-up on the 1.0: https://developer.chrome.com/blog/modern-web-guidance-v1 --- 0: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50416456 1: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/modern-web-guidance/guides 2: https://googlechrome.github.io/modern-web-guidance-src/

items.summary: See how Workday used LangGraph and LangSmith to build an internal AI agent platform that cut prototype time from months to less than a day and compliance needs.
items.story_key: model:langgraph|title:how workday built an enterprise scale ai agent platform with langgraph and langs
items.content_excerpt: Workday is the trusted agentic platform for HR, finance, and IT, serving more than half the Fortune 500. The team set out to create the internal developer platform to build, deploy, and run AI agents in production, on Workday's infrastructure. The team leveraged LangGraph for agent orchestration and LangSmith for tracing, observability, and evals. In 2025, Workday’s leadership team saw the market opportunity for building agentic solutions and set an ambitious goal for agents in production by the end of 2026. Product teams needed a platform that could support both rapid prototyping and production deployments—a uniquely challenging mandate given Workday operates under some of the strictest security and data governance requirements in enterprise software. Getting any internal service into production means satisfying demanding audit, compliance, and data retention policies. The surface area was enormous for a team of four, encompassing a durable, scalable agent server; data access controls tied to Workday's audit policies; a collaborative eval platform; and an SDK that abstracted all of it. Workday’s Agent Platform team serves two user bases. 1.) the internal Workday engineering teams building agents, and 2.) the end customers of those agents. It lets teams focus on functional requirements, while handling authentication, security, compliance, and infrastructure. The first major product shipped was Workday's Agent System of Record, a governance layer that controls which APIs the agents are allowed to access. The Agent Platform team built the backend server and eval infrastructure that the system of record runs on top of. The team also built what Alex Gatto, Senior Machine Learning Engineer, describes as "Workday LangChain": a Python SDK that wraps LangChain primitives and routes them through Workday's internal services, including an LLM gateway, a RAG retrieval service, and other internal tooling. "Anytime there was some AI concept that LangChain had put out, we tried to build a Python SDK for that same concept, but at Workday," explained Alex. Workday chose LangGraph for agent orchestration to give internal developers maximum flexibility at the design layer, while providing standardized infrastructure underneath. items.content_excerpt: Developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers can now try our latest frontier model. Today, we’re making Gemini 4 Carbon available to developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers. Carbon is our strongest model with frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows across complex knowledge work, software engineering, and scientific reasoning. Two weeks ago , we released Carbon to a set of cybersecurity defenders via our Fairwind Program . Following our recent launch of Gemini 4 Argon , Carbon pushes the frontier even further. Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence like complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery — using more tokens than Argon to explore thoroughly, reason deeply, and run extended verification loops. Across independent benchmarks designed to test model performance in real workflows, Carbon pairs frontier accuracy with practical production economics. It ranks #1 on CursorBench 4.0 , Perplexity’s WANDR , and Zapier’s AutomationBench at more than 2X lower cost per task compared to the next best external model. To put Carbon’s capabilities to work on larger and complex projects, we’re previewing /swarm in Google Antigravity, turning a single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time. Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change. Gemini 4 Carbon is available via the API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business for all paying developers and enterprises, at the same introductory price 1 as Gemini 4 Argon ($2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens). It is also rolling out to all Google AI Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , the Gemini app , and AI Mode in Search . Across legal, finance, and enterprise operations, Gemini 4 Carbon combines frontier visual understanding, reasoning, and exhaustive retrieval to synthesize grounded insights across large sets of dense documents and data. items.title: What a read-only Postgres role does and doesn't stop when an AI agent connects
items.story_key: story|title:what a read only postgres role does and doesn t stop when an ai agent connects
items.content_excerpt: A reproducible run on PostgreSQL 17.11: the careful role, the errors it produces, the settings any session can turn off, and the reads that still do harm. AI agents now hold database credentials. Coding agents read DATABASE_URL from the project, MCP servers expose a query tool, and text-to-SQL features run whatever a model writes. In 2026 there were public reports of agents dropping tables and columns in production; we collected 13 documented cases, with sources, in an earlier post . The usual first answer is a read-only role, and it is the right place to start. This post checks what such a role does on PostgreSQL 17, statement by statement: which errors it produces, which of its settings a session can turn off, and which reads it allows that you may not want an agent to make. Disclosure. We build Vericto, so we have a stake in this topic. Everything below is plain PostgreSQL, with no Vericto component in the path. Every output was copied from a real run; the commands are in the appendix. A throwaway postgres:17 container (17.11) on its own Docker network, with no published ports, and a second container on the same network as the client. Every session in this post is psql 17.11 over TCP with password authentication, run with -e so each statement is echoed above its result. The database shop belongs to app_owner and has three tables: customers (with name, email and phone), orders , split between tenants 42 and 7, and api_keys . There is also one helper function, refund_order(int) , written the way many applications write them: SECURITY DEFINER with a pinned search_path . The agent's task is to answer questions about orders and customers. This is the role, created the way a careful checklist would create it, as a superuser: REVOKE CREATE ON SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC changes nothing on a database created by PostgreSQL 15 or later, where the public schema is owned by pg_database_owner and only the database owner can create objects in it. The schemas chapter puts it this way: “In databases upgraded from PostgreSQL 14 or earlier, everyone has that privilege on the schema public.” If your database came through pg_upgrade from 14 or earlier, you need it. The schema ACL after the grant: The role attributes NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE NOBYPASSRLS are already the defaults of CREATE ROLE . NaiveAI could potentially top Artificial Analysis’s speed rankings. Our hands-on test suggests its coding quality holds up against DeepSeek. Editor’s note: With this post, we are launching a new series focused on trying new models and products with unbiased reviews. Reach out with suggestions to tips@latent.space. Naive-N0.5-Flash is a new open-weights model built for AI coding tasks and tuned to generate as many tokens per second as possible . It was developed by a Chinese company called NaiveAI , with the aim of speeding up engineering and research workflows so that teams can experiment, iterate and solve complex problems faster. The model is an evolution of Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.5 , which NaiveAI has trained further for long-context reasoning and paired with its own NaiveRT inference engine. Naive-N0.5-Flash arrives with a bold pitch: a model built largely by AI and trained to do AI research itself, with recursive self-improvement as the long-term goal. To see what changed, it helps to know where it started. MiMo-V2.5 is a 310B-parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 15B active parameters, trained on 48T tokens. Its language backbone inherits the hybrid design of MiMo-V2-Flash, which mixes sliding-window attention (SWA) with global self-attention. NaiveAI's recipe starts from those weights. Through continued, multi-stage training, the team adapted the checkpoint to DeepSeek Sparse Attention layers. According to the NaiveAI technical blog , this took roughly 3.25T additional tokens on top of MiMo's original 48T. About 3T of those additional tokens were trained at a fixed 1M context length and with a constant learning rate. We benchmarked the ultrafast mode of Naive-N0.5-Flash against DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash , and then gave all three the same app-building prompts. The trade-off, we discovered, is that Naive-N0.5-Flash takes longer to reason through harder problems, yet it still delivers answers faster overall. However, that comes at a slightly higher cost per question — although that may be an acceptable price for applications where speed comes first. items.content_excerpt: Define semantics once in Unity Catalog and publish them directly to Power BI semantic models Organizations want a single, trusted definition of their business semantics. Revenue, margin, and active customers should mean the same thing in every report, notebook, and AI application. When they don't, business users and AI agents read the same data differently and reach different answers. Finance and sales show different revenue numbers, teams lose trust in their reports, and decisions get made on the wrong numbers. Unity Catalog metric views , part of Unity Catalog semantics, solve this by enabling customers to define business KPIs once in Databricks, in an open, governed semantic layer that sits on top of the lakehouse. At the same time, many of these organizations rely on Power BI as the front end for their business users. Often, organizations have thousands of PowerBI workspaces each with its own Semantic Models, creating a governance and unification nightmare. Furthermore, when each team builds its own metrics and relationships in Power BI, the same logic lives in many places. Reports drift apart, and every definition change means updating each copy. Customers have told us they want both: Databricks as their unified, open semantic layer, and Power BI as their front end. With Publish to Power BI , they can now have both. Every Power BI report uses the same governed UC metric views as AI/BI dashboards and Genie, so teams work from consistent numbers. Business users can build self-serve reports and explore metrics across any dimension without waiting on a data team to model data or write DAX. Data teams maintain one definition in Databricks instead of many copies across systems. Publish on demand from Catalog Explorer, or add a Power BI task to a Lakeflow Job to keep metric views and semantic models in sync in production. With Publish to Power BI or a Power BI task, you can connect Unity Catalog metric views to a Power BI semantic model. Each metric view becomes a table in the model. The metric view’s dimensions (aka Fields) become columns and its measures become DAX measures. Power BI queries the metric view itself (as if it was a table). The metric view stays the source of truth, and joins defined in the metric view run in Databricks. Joined dimensions, such as campaign channel or region, show up in Power BI as ordinary columns, so you don't have to rebuild table relationships in Power BI. items.content_excerpt: Kubernetes, the open source system that manages how applications run across thousands of AI factories, has become the foundation for AI, and the demands on it are only growing. To help meet them, NVIDIA is deepening its commitment to open source at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon , the flagship conference for the Kubernetes and cloud-native communities. NVIDIA is contributing NVIDIA OpenShell , an open source runtime for securing and governing autonomous agents, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), a nonprofit that is part of the Linux Foundation and the host of KubeCon. As a CNCF Sandbox project, OpenShell will be governed by the organizations building it into their products and strengthened by the expertise of security professionals worldwide. NVIDIA is also contributing to Agent Substrate , an open source Google-led framework for operating long-running agent workloads at scale on Kubernetes that has been accepted into the CNCF Sandbox. Additionally, NVIDIA announced new components of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform : NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine , NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes and NVIDIA Snapshot . These tools help teams deploy, manage and scale GPU infrastructure on Kubernetes for AI factories. Together, these advancements mark a step forward in making Kubernetes the leading foundation for AI workloads at scale — empowering developers to build safer, more efficient AI infrastructure for the future. NVIDIA’s contribution of OpenShell to CNCF puts security infrastructure for autonomous agents in the community’s hands to build, inspect and improve — accelerating development and hardening its safeguards. “The cloud-native community has a new infrastructure challenge: giving agents secure environments in which to operate,” said Jim Zemlin, CEO of the Linux Foundation. “NVIDIA’s contribution of OpenShell to CNCF gives developers a shared foundation to build on and an opportunity to shape how agent security evolves. Bringing this work into the community enables broader collaboration on infrastructure that will be critical to the next generation of cloud-native applications.” OpenShell gives organizations control over what AI agents can do. It applies deterministic controls to agent activity, so teams can enforce policies as agents use tools, access inference services and execute workloads. items.title: What Is Eval-Driven Development? How to Improve AI Agents
items.summary: Eval-driven development helps you build AI agents against a consistent set of metrics. Define good behavior, write the eval first, then compare experiments.
items.story_key: story|title:what is eval driven development how to improve ai agents
items.content_excerpt: Development on most agents starts the same way. You write a prompt, try a few questions by hand, adjust, and try again. This works well in the beginning, when agent errors are obvious and improvements are easy to see. But over time it becomes increasingly difficult to know whether your most recent change made an agent better or worse. Eval-driven development (EDD) solves this by giving you a consistent set of metrics to measure your agent’s performance against and guide your decision making. Here at LangChain we've used EDD when building our most advanced agents (check out our blog on IssueBench ), and have boiled it down to a three step process: In this blog, we'll walk through this process step by step so that your team can apply it to your own agent development process. The name and concept of eval-driven development borrows from test-driven development (TDD), where you write a failing test before writing the code that passes it. Agents differ from traditional code as they're non-deterministic: As a result, agents need a different kind of test. An eval handles this by scoring runs of your agent across a set of examples. Evals are more flexible than traditional testing. You can score any aspect of the agent's run and you can use other LLMs to score it ( LLM-as-a-judge ). With EDD, similar to TDD, these evals become your definition of success and you build your agent towards them. The first step in EDD is defining what your agent should do. Then, list the behaviors it needs to handle to get there. These could be tasks such as answering questions from a knowledge base, taking an action on a user's behalf, or knowing when to ask a follow-up question. Write down the requirements for each behavior. Together, these make up a product requirements document (PRD) for your agent. EDD works on one behavior at a time. This gives you a narrow target to hill climb toward, without one change muddying the effect of another. The behavior you pick usually comes from a feature you're about to build or a failure you found in your agent's past runs. Before writing code, it’s helpful to define a short spec that covers: Say we have an internal docs agent that employees query for company information. It has two tools: search_docs for internal documentation and web_search for everything else. We plan to add a create_ticket tool so it can file IT tickets. items.title: Shortcuts and Boundaries: Verifiable RL Misalignment and Contextual Safety Learning
items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve an agent's task capability while reinforcing behavior that violates contextual execution requirements. We study this reward-driven misalignment, including reward hacking, through verifiable reward--context conflicts, where compliant task completion remains feasible while some executable shortcuts earn more reward than every compliant strategy. Encoding these conflicts in task dynamics lets us generate diverse interactive environments at scale and derive compliance feedback from execution histories. In resource and reporting workflows, task optimization increases real productivity through unauthorized resource use or raises reported scores while actual work declines. Controlled changes in the training distribution show that minority conflict exposure can still lead to widespread shortcut acquisition, reaching 97.9\% certified profitable violations on an API task under a 25\% conflict mixture after 128 updates. The same contextual checks supply a simple binary penalty that supports joint capability and compliance gains and partially mitigates acquired violations. Learned safety adapts to expanded authorization and transfers across mechanisms into workflows with evolving evidence and approval requirements. On 32 unseen changing-evidence tasks, resource-trained safety increases safe completion from 53.1\% to 89.1\% relative to task-only training, while both policies achieve full real work. These results connect a verifiable account of reward-driven misalignment with scalable task construction and safety learning that remains useful under changing execution requirements.

items.title: AgentOPSD: Turn-Level Credit Assignment via Recursive Belief Revision
items.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards ordinarily spreads a single advantage over a whole trajectory, a granularity too coarse to isolate the few decisions on which success in a long, multi-turn interaction actually turns. Privileged self-distillation supplies denser supervision, but it leaves unanswered how a set of local teacher-student discrepancies should be converted into credit along a sequence. We introduce AgentOPSD, a critic-free scheme that assigns credit recursively, one interaction turn at a time. Inside a turn, the token-level log-probability gaps between a skill-conditioned self-teacher and the student are summed, and that sum acts as evidence in a recursive Bayesian update carried out in log-odds space; the resulting revisions reallocate the outcome-derived advantage across turns through a multiplier that is bounded and preserves its sign. With Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-7B as policy backbones on ALFWorld, the method improves consistently on GRPO and on self-distillation baselines, and attains 89.1% success at the 7B scale. Ablations attribute the gain to aggregating evidence at turn boundaries and to making the belief revision depend on history, rather than to the local gap by itself.

items.title: Adaptive Quantization Preserves Fast Rates for TD Learning over Rate-Limited Channels
items.summary: Motivated by reinforcement learning subject to communication constraints, we study a policy evaluation problem with linear function approximation over a rate-limited channel. In our setup, an agent interacting with an unknown environment (modeled as a Markov Decision Process) transmits quantized estimates of a temporal-difference (TD) learning update direction to a server over a finite-capacity channel. Our goal is to investigate to what extent one can preserve the statistical convergence rates achievable when the channel has infinite capacity. To that end, we propose a new algorithm called Batched Adaptively Quantized TD (BAQ-TD), which uses batching to reduce the variance of the transmitted information, and adaptive quantization to encode innovations. We prove a high-probability finite-time error bound for BAQ-TD, and show that, above a certain finite channel capacity, BAQ-TD preserves the convergence rate of unquantized TD up to logarithmic factors. Specifically, for a $d$-dimensional value function parameter, we establish that transmitting a total of $\mathcal{O}(d \log(T))$ bits over a horizon of length $T$ suffices to achieve the order-optimal rate of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/T)$, marking an exponential improvement in communication-complexity over prior work.

items.title: Fisher-Glass Learning: Classification Bounds and Subpopulation Audits
items.summary: Accurate classifiers can fail when background cues change without altering the correct labels. Predictive performance alone does not quantify how much task information remains after accounting for such nuisance variation. Here we extend the Fisher-glass framework to connect nuisance-adjusted information with local classification difficulty and subpopulation auditing. We derive lower bounds on local minimax excess classification risk under explicit distinguishability and decision-separation conditions, alongside statistical audits accounting for estimation error and regularization. On Waterbirds, a feature-based diagnostic of task-background alignment selects an accurately classified group, with selection frozen before held-out evaluation. Across five training seeds, background replacements preserving the extracted bird foreground and labels yield 93.2% accuracy when background type is preserved and 40.6% when it changes, a controlled difference of 52.6 percentage points. Separately, search using task labels and a fixed nuisance direction identifies an independently evaluated population with 98.8% membership-weighted accuracy and low estimated projected predictive Fisher information. Training and acquisition experiments show that information gains and predictive gains can diverge. These findings support joint assessment of predictive performance, information under declared nuisance models and controlled sensitivity when diagnosing vulnerability and evaluating model improvements.

items.title: Vendi Anomaly Scores for Efficient and Accurate Anomaly Detection
items.summary: Anomaly detection (AD) is a critical for trustworthy machine learning and scientific discovery. Existing methods typically define anomalies through local density, isolation heuristics, or distance from a fitted distribution, making them sensitive to neighborhood scale, partitioning choices, or restrictive distributional assumptions. In this work, we introduce a new paradigm by formulating anomaly detection from a diversity perspective. We propose the $\textit{Vendi Anomaly Score}$ (VAS), which detects anomalies by quantifying how much a sample changes the diversity of the dataset, as measured by the Vendi score, when removed. VAS captures both local redundancy and global data structure without relying on density estimation or partitioning heuristics. Moreover, VAS requires no hyperparameter tuning, instead adapting automatically to the spectral structure of the data. VAS is non-parametric and scales linearly with dataset size. Across 148 benchmark embedding datasets derived from 10 source datasets and 4 embedding architectures, VAS achieves state-of-the-art AD performance. We further validate VAS on large-scale ImageNet experiments, where it remains robust as both contamination rate and dataset scale increase.

items.title: claude-code v2.1.321
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added Claude Fable 5.2 (claude-fable-5-2), now the default Fable model — 1M context, $8/$40 per Mtok with $0.20/Mtok cache reads
  • Added --settings <file> to claude remote-control, which applies a settings file to every session it starts; if the file changes, no new session starts until you restart claude remote-control
  • Fixed MCP OAuth requests sending secrets such as refresh tokens to another host when a server redirected them
  • Fixed a case where a read-only Bash command ran outside the sandbox without a permission prompt
  • Fixed a case where Bash permission checks judged a file write from the wrong folder and didn't prompt
  • Fixed deny rules and protected-file prompts not applying to the file that a cp or mv into a directory writes
  • Fixed the "Draws from usage credits" note showing after a switch to Fable on Enterprise seats whose plan includes Fable
  • Fixed the fallback model sometimes declining a request or mentioning a stopped response when the first model was blocked before replying
  • Fixed claude mcp login printing a SEP-2352 issuer warning each time you sign in again to a server that Claude Code registered with
  • Fixed NotebookEdit deleting or overwriting a notebook's first cell when the call named no cell, on network paths (UNC shares, WSL folders, /net mounts)
  • Fixed Edit changing the first of several matches, replacing a whole file on an empty old_string, or editing a notebook as text, on network paths (UNC shares, WSL folders, /net mounts)
  • Fixed /config showing Manual as the default permission mode when new sessions start in auto mode; pressing Space on "Auto (default)" now saves Don't Ask, not Plan
  • Windows: Fixed FileChanged hooks stopping for paths set through watchPaths after the first shell command, when the session's working directory had a lowercase drive letter
  • Fixed --plugin-dir . and --plugin-dir ./builtin writing generated type files for Claude Code's built-in plugins into a builtin folder
  • Fixed context usage estimates overcounting tool definitions when exact token counts are unavailable
  • Fixed /compact showing twice in Remote Control on web and mobile
  • Fixed plugin auto-updates and /plugin marketplace updates downloading a plugin again for each worktree or folder of a repository
  • Fixed auto mode losing a background subagent's report that had started a turn when the conversation was compacted before Claude answered it
  • Fixed project skills, commands and agents staying missing after their folder was removed and came back mid-session, such as with git stash, including after entering a worktree
  • Fixed claude -p sometimes telling Claude that background commands get 30 minutes when they are stopped after 10
  • Fixed pkill, pgrep and pidwait in cloud sessions matching the session's own parent processes
  • Fixed Claude in Chrome and computer use server processes staying alive after their parent exits behind a proxy that stalls connections
  • Fixed a large hook output pointing Claude to a file that held another hook's output from the same tool call
  • Fixed apps that embed Claude Code getting their own PreToolUse hook's ask reason instead of another hook's when both asked
  • Fixed a PreToolUse hook's ask being lost when another hook's defer finished first and could not be honored
  • Fixed a rare crash on permission prompts and background tasks
  • Fixed project skills, commands and agents disappearing from the menu in SDK and desktop sessions after Claude entered a worktree
  • Fixed /desktop on macOS saying Claude Desktop is not installed when it is in ~/Applications
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry repository attributes (vcs.*) missing from Claude Desktop sessions that start on a pre-started process
  • Fixed WebFetch passing "No response from model" to Claude as page content when the model reading the page returned no text; the call now fails with a clear error
  • Fixed screen reader mode delaying the prompt at startup when the system clock moved back while Claude Code was starting
  • Fixed a command's panel sometimes not coming back after a dialog closed, leaving no panel or prompt on screen until the next redraw
  • Fixed a project's MCP server being disconnected after the first message in a Claude Desktop Code tab session when the desktop app has an MCP server or extension of the same name
  • Fixed a turn ending with "API Error: EPROTO: The TLS handshake failed" when the connection broke partway through a reply; the partial reply is kept or the request is retried, as before 2.1.302
  • Fixed high memory use in long sessions that repeatedly read single lines from large files
  • Fixed fast mode losing replies, switching models or retrying for minutes when fast serving is rate-limited, overloaded or failing; it now tries standard speed on the same model first
  • Fixed one request carrying far more background agent reports than intended after Claude was stopped while several were waiting
  • Fixed messages from a Claude Desktop Code tab session to your other sessions staying paused after you typed while Claude was still working
  • Fixed claude agents ignoring --permission-mode, --dangerously-skip-permissions, --model, --effort or --agent typed before agents when a flag such as --verbose was also on the line
  • Fixed a case where Remote Control showed as off with "login expired" in the desktop app while its connection was still up, because the app was briefly unable to hand over a sign-in token
  • Fixed a Remote Control message sent with "Queue for later" reaching Claude in the middle of the running turn
  • Fixed the git status given to Claude at session start reading as clean when git status failed; it now reads as unavailable
  • Fixed the git status given to Claude at session start showing the first listed file as staged when its changes were not staged
  • Fixed a hang or out-of-memory crash when a connector in a cloud session lists resources with very long names
  • Fixed Remote Control showing as connected after its connection closed for good while the session's history was still uploading
  • Fixed screen reader mode turning off when you return to a conversation from agent view
  • Fixed screen reader mode y/n questions taking as yes a stray "y" at the end of text typed as the question opened
  • Fixed cloud sessions telling Claude that a host is probably not allowed when it is allowed and the network proxy could not connect to it
  • Fixed an MCP server sometimes showing as connected with no tools after it was reconnected or the session's directory changed while its tools were still loading
  • Fixed Bash commands sometimes running in the wrong folder when Claude sent several at once and an earlier one changed folders
  • Fixed files Claude sends from cloud and Remote Control sessions failing at once when an upload gets an HTTP 507 from a proxy; the upload now gets a second try
  • Fixed new messages not being saved, and claude -p, SDK and VS Code sessions hanging, when memory ran out while the transcript was being read
  • Fixed sign-in, token refresh and logout waiting indefinitely when something on the network accepts the connection but never answers the TLS handshake
  • Fixed a sent file showing under a different name in the Claude apps when its name hid text-direction or control characters; Claude now refuses to send such a file
  • Fixed sub-agent progress summaries running a request to its end after the model replied with a tool call
  • Fixed Bash reads such as grep -r foo "$PWD/src" asking for permission when the same command with the path typed out runs without asking
  • Fixed Claude apps gateway refusing to start when a desktop setting holds a field newer than the gateway, such as a managed MCP server's oauth.omitResource; it now warns and serves it
  • Fixed Bash commands coming back empty for zsh users whose .zshrc sets KSH_OPTION_PRINT
  • macOS: Fixed "Unable to read managed policy settings" at startup when a valid MDM profile was slow to read: the read is retried once, and a timeout is now reported as a timeout
  • Fixed agent view erasing another agent view's saved input text when it restarted for an update with nothing typed
  • Fixed remote sessions giving no reply after a restart when a UserPromptSubmit hook blocked a replayed permission answer; these hooks no longer run on that replay
  • Fixed claude remote-control accepting a y typed without Enter at its first-run question when the terminal's input ended
  • Fixed Claude Desktop not showing spend limit warnings behind a Claude apps gateway whose policy has no code: rules
  • Fixed fullscreen sessions with some plugins ending with an error when a tool result that had got shorter scrolled off the top of the screen
  • Fixed prompt suggestions making extra API requests when the model replied with a tool call
  • Fixed PreToolUse mcp_tool hooks on stdio and HTTP MCP servers being skipped when their answer was over 16 MiB; the tool call is now refused
  • Fixed skill and command names holding a Bamum letter that some fonts draw as blank: they are now refused
  • Fixed claude -p on Linux exiting 0 in silence when a full NFS export or a used-up NFS quota lost transcript lines: it now prints an error and, in text and json output, exits 1
  • Fixed background agents being reported as stopped by the user, and refused a resume, when a service interrupted a cloud session and nobody pressed Stop
  • Fixed NotebookEdit reporting success to hooks and telemetry when the edit failed, for example when the notebook changed while the permission prompt was open
  • Fixed a blank screen or no answer at startup, and empty claude mcp list output, when a stored MCP sign-in record was null
  • Fixed the Artifact tool telling Claude to add filters when an artifact's database collection is too large to sort; it now says to read the collection page by page and sort the results
  • Fixed a restarted cloud session dropping a message with a large image when the restart came before Claude's first reply to it
  • Fixed a restarted cloud session leaving a subagent's message to the main conversation unanswered
  • Fixed Claude not being told when you stop or pause a running workflow, so it no longer says the workflow is still running
  • Improved the /model picker: "More models" is now an unnumbered row below every other, and older models open under it without renumbering the rest
  • Gateway: Improved spend limits on a busy replica, which now skips fewer checks and records spend sooner
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's sign-in limit messages in Claude Code and on the /device page: they no longer name gateway settings, which the gateway's own log still names
  • Improved claude install and the install scripts: they finish 2 to 4 seconds sooner
  • Improved how soon a Remote Control session whose process crashed can pick up a new message
  • Windows: Improved startup and first-command time by finding programs on PATH without starting a helper process
  • Improved auto mode in headless sessions, the desktop app and VS Code: reports from background subagents that wait together are answered in one model call, as in the terminal
  • Improved the agent view's row for a claude --bg --worktree session that couldn't set up its worktree: it now shows the error from its beginning, not an internal tag or its last 200 characters
  • Improved the messages shown when an artifact is in another organization: /login is offered only if it's one of yours, and Claude now says where a copy may be after an account move
  • Improved sessions with more images than fit in one request: Claude is told whether it has already seen a dropped image, and repeat reads of an unchanged image are limited
  • Improved claude remote-control's messages for an unanswered first-run question: each now says what to do next
  • Improved start-up time by loading trusted TLS certificates faster
  • Improved Claude apps gateway error messages to show the gateway's address without any user name or password
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's spend limit error: the reset now shows in your local time, such as "resets 4pm (America/Los_Angeles)"
  • Windows: Improved startup time with a standard Git for Windows install by no longer checking which git.exe to run on every launch
  • Updated the session-feedback message and the allowedProviders setting description to name Ultra alongside Pro and Max, and the forceLoginMethod description to cover every paid Claude plan
  • Updated the bundled dataviz skill to suggest a list of meters, one row per item, for several ratios that each have their own limit
  • Updated the "Upgrade to Max" options to say "Upgrade to Max or Ultra"
  • Changed mods Claude writes to turn on without asking in auto and bypass modes, even with managed allowUnsandboxedCommands: false or allowManagedDomainsOnly, and not to load in dontAsk mode
  • Changed mods' own tool calls ($.tool.call, $.mcp.call) to raise no permission prompt, even under your own ask rules or in dontAsk and -p runs; deny rules and organization policy still apply
  • Changed saved Fable 5.1 model picks to move to fable: on Pro and Max plans at once, on Team and Enterprise plans once your organization allows it; use /model claude-fable-5-1 to switch back
  • Changed the fast mode labels in /fast, /config and /model to name your current model when it supports fast mode, and removed "(Opus only)" from the VS Code row
  • Changed nested skill loading: .claude/skills folders inside ~/.claude/plugins no longer load when Claude works on files there
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed an on-demand runner that the server refuses because it is not needed (session ended or paused, work order superseded) to exit 0 instead of 1
  • Windows: Changed how Claude Code finds programs it starts itself, such as git, to skip relative and UNC PATH entries and links onto a network share, and to pick up PATH changes from settings
  • Changed OpenTelemetry hook events in non-interactive sessions to leave two built-in hooks out of num_hooks and num_success after Bash and PowerShell calls
  • Changed the number of messages a Claude Desktop Code tab session can send to your other sessions before it waits for you to type again from 10 to 20
  • Changed AskUserQuestion in claude -p and SDK sessions to deny a host's permission answer that sets the undocumented afkTimeoutMs input field
  • Changed managed extraKnownMarketplaces: a declared name can't be added from another source, an entry from elsewhere is hidden, and plugins the declared marketplace lists are reinstalled from it
  • Changed Claude in Chrome tools that an app running Claude Code provides, such as the Claude desktop app's Code tab, to follow your organization's Claude in Chrome policy
  • Changed policy_mode: layered in the Claude apps gateway: managed MCP servers now add up over every matching policy, match: {} included, so a gateway already on it serves more after the upgrade
  • Gateway: Changed Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry upstreams to ignore the ANTHROPIC_*_BASE_URL variables in the gateway's environment. Set base_url on the upstream to use another endpoint
  • Changed headless sessions to reload mods in .claude/skills when their files change; set CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIR_WATCH=0 to turn this off
  • Changed the Cyber Verification Program sentence on a cyber safeguard block to use the same words as claude.ai
  • Changed Cowork cloud sessions: a PostToolUse hook can no longer replace the answer to AskUserQuestion or the plan in ExitPlanMode's result; Claude reads the originals
  • Changed cp and mv spelled by a path, such as /bin/cp, to get the same path checks as cp and mv
  • Changed background command notifications and TaskStop results to show Claude only the start and end of a command over 1,000 characters, which saves context
  • Changed artifact design guidance to treat Inter and Space Grotesk as good default typefaces
  • Changed the account email check to refuse only a shell command that holds your email and names a User-Agent, without asking, so other commands and scheduled runs no longer stop at its prompt
  • Changed Remote Control sessions to keep the folder they were started in: a connected client can no longer move a session to another folder
  • Changed managed extraKnownMarketplaces take-overs from an undeclared source: saved data is set aside for cleanupPeriodDays, and options and secrets until claude plugin restore-set-aside
  • [VSCode] Added a warning above the prompt box when both an auth token and an API key are set, matching the terminal's startup warning
  • [VSCode] Fixed a plugin's permission request showing a name with hidden characters: it now reads "a plugin"
